title: Majestic King Cage: Use the Opponent’s Blockers
summary: Recognize a smothered mate before taking a valuable piece that opens the cage.

nodes.question: White has only a knight. Why is the black king still in danger?
nodes.explanation: Begin after ...Qxa6 at 101 seconds. White has Ke7 and Nb4; Black has Ka7, Qa6, Ba8, Nb7 and b6. Four adjacent squares are occupied by black pieces; the checking knight can cover the remaining b8 flight.

branches.title: Source finish: check the caged king
commentary: The source’s earlier bishop, pawn and queen sacrifices have produced this complete seven-piece diagram. Only the final decision and comparison are checked here.

Nc6# checks Ka7 with the knight. Black’s own Qa6, Ba8, Nb7 and b6 pawn occupy a6, a8, b7 and b6, and Nc6 itself controls the remaining b8 flight. A knight check cannot be interposed against, and none of the black pieces can capture Nc6. The boxed-in king is checkmated.

branches.title: Independent error: take the queen and open the cage
commentary: An independently selected comparison tests the tempting material capture instead of giving mate.
Nxa6 removes the queen but gives up the forced win. The knight has left b4 without checking Ka7 and is now adjacent to the king.

Kxa6 captures the knight and opens the cage by removing the white attacker. Black has a checked win with bishop, knight and pawn against the lone white king. The higher-value capture lost the mating opportunity.

exercises.prompt: Why does a queen help trap its own king here?
exercises.answer: Qa6 occupies a flight square without being able to capture the checking knight on c6. Ba8, Nb7 and b6 fill three more exits; the knight on c6 controls the remaining b8 square.

exercises.prompt: Why is taking the queen worse than making the knight check?
exercises.answer: Nxa6 lets the king take White’s last piece. Nc6 instead gives an unblockable knight check while Black’s own pieces block four exits and the checking knight covers b8.
